questions.title: Section A — Question 1 (Case study: Pioneer White butterfly migration)

subQuestions.questionText:
The source describes the migration of the Pioneer White butterfly (Belenois aurota) from the Kalahari, its life cycle on the Shepherd Bush (Boscia albitrunca), its predators (including robber flies), and two investigations into its numbers. Provide a word from the text that means the same as each statement:
1.1.1 A group of individuals of the same species occurring in the same area.
1.1.2 Organisms that are able to produce fertile offspring with one another.
1.1.3 The number of individuals of a species that can live in an area without environmental degradation occurring.
subQuestions.memoText:
1.1.1 Population
1.1.2 Species
1.1.3 Carrying capacity
(1 mark each)

subQuestions.questionText:
The word 'niche' is used in ecological studies.
1.2.1 Explain the meaning of the word niche.
1.2.2 The life cycle of Pioneer White butterflies (metamorphosis) has advantages for their survival. Referring to metamorphosis, suggest and explain some of these advantages.
subQuestions.memoText:
1.2.1 (2 marks) The ecological role / position / function of a species in its ecosystem — how it interacts with the biotic and abiotic components of its habitat and the combination of factors that allow it to survive (NOT simply "its environment").
1.2.2 (3 marks — any 3 facts, or one fact well explained): the adult and larva occupy different niches, so they do not compete for the same food → higher survival; the winged adult can disperse to new areas, reducing competition; adult and larva have different predators, spreading predation risk; the chrysalis protects the developing insect; overwintering in different habitats reduces competition and predation.

subQuestions.questionText:
Figure 1.1 shows four South African butterfly species (A–D), each with its own scale bar (A: 10 mm, B: 20 mm, C: 3 mm, D: 7 mm; images NOT to the same scale). The Pioneer White has white wings with brown patterns on the front wings and brown veins on the hindwings, and a wingspan of 50 mm. Using the data and the article, decide which butterfly (A, B, C or D) is a Pioneer White. Explain TWO reasons for your answer.
(Refer to Figure 1.1 in the source booklet.)
subQuestions.memoText: A (1 — correct choice). Reasons (mark first 2 only): the wing pattern matches the text — white with brown patterning on the forewings and brown veins on the hindwings (1); using the scale bar, the wingspan works out to about 50 mm as described (measured length ÷ scale-bar length × scale value ≈ 50 mm) (1).

subQuestions.questionText: Is the migration of the butterflies from the Kalahari an emigration or an immigration?
subQuestions.memoText: Emigration (individuals leaving/moving out of the Kalahari population).

subQuestions.questionText: Use the information in the sources to explain ONE reason why the Shepherd Bush provides an ideal place for the butterfly to lay its eggs.
subQuestions.memoText: One concept explained (2 marks): the Shepherd Bush is evergreen / stays green in winter, so the leaves carrying the eggs do not fall off and there is a continuous, immediate food source for the caterpillars as soon as they hatch. OR the tree's shade keeps the eggs/larvae cooler and protects them from high temperatures, aiding survival. (A single phrase with no explanation earns 1 mark.)

subQuestions.questionText: Use the information in the text and your own knowledge to explain the possible effect of climate change on the future numbers of Pioneer White butterflies migrating from the Kalahari.
subQuestions.memoText: A described climate scenario (wetter/drier/hotter/colder) linked to an effect on numbers and to migration (3 marks). Example — higher numbers emigrating: drier conditions → fewer leaves on the Shepherd Bush / more leaves used by farmers as fodder or eaten by other species → more competition for food and water → more pressure on butterflies to emigrate. OR lower numbers emigrating: less water/food means fewer larvae survive to become adults, so fewer emigrate; or fewer predators means less pressure to leave.

subQuestions.questionText:
Quadrats are an indirect method used to assess population numbers of organisms. In Investigation 1, three 200 m × 200 m sites (A, B, C), each divided into 20 m × 20 m quadrats, were sampled by three student groups; Shepherd Bush distribution differed at each site (Figure 1.9).
1.7.1 What is meant by an "indirect" sampling method of population assessment?
1.7.2 Evaluate the reliability of the placement of the sampled quadrats at each site A, B and C. State clearly the site where the most reliable method of sampling was used.
(Refer to Figure 1.9 in the source booklet.)
subQuestions.memoText:
1.7.1 (2 marks): a method in which only a sample (a few quadrats) of the population is counted and the total is then estimated/extrapolated by calculation, rather than counting every individual.
1.7.2 (4 marks): Site A — most reliable, because the quadrats were placed randomly and spread across the site, giving a representative sample; Site B — not reliable, only one quadrat was sampled, so it is not representative and no average can be found; Site C — not reliable, the quadrats were not placed randomly (biased placement).

subQuestions.questionText:
Figure 1.5 shows total rainfall in the Northern Cape from 2017 to 2020 together with the population numbers of Pioneer White butterflies and robber flies in the area.
1.8.1 Identify the organism represented by line A.
1.8.2 Use the graph to explain how rainfall is a limiting factor for the population numbers of robber flies.
(Refer to Figure 1.5 in the source booklet.)
subQuestions.memoText:
1.8.1 A = the Pioneer White butterfly (1).
1.8.2 (2 marks): as rainfall decreases there are fewer leaves on the trees, so fewer butterflies hatch and develop (less food); with fewer butterflies as prey, robber fly numbers also fall — rainfall acts as a limiting factor because it prevents further growth of the robber fly population.

subQuestions.questionText: What might a game ranger in the Mokala National Park observe about Shepherd Bushes that would indicate that the carrying capacity for the Pioneer White butterflies has been reached?
subQuestions.memoText: Any ONE: the Shepherd Bushes have few / badly damaged / no leaves left (bare trees) / all the leaves are covered in eggs — there is not enough food left for the caterpillars.

subQuestions.questionText: Consider the "windscreen study" (Investigation 2, Figure 1.10) in which the public was asked, via social media, to report the number of Pioneer White butterflies killed on their car windscreens. Provide THREE reasons why this data collection will not lead to valid results.
subQuestions.memoText: Any 3 (1 mark each): most butterflies fly more than 3 m above the ground, so many are never hit or counted; it is hard to count squashed butterflies that overlap or fall off the windscreen; members of the public are not trained to identify butterfly species; other insects on the windscreen may be miscounted as butterflies; not everyone uses social media / owns a car, so the sample is biased; the method is not repeatable; the study area and sampling period are not defined.

questions.title: Section A — Question 2 (Case study: dung beetles)

subQuestions.questionText:
The source describes dung beetles — how they use herbivore dung for food and egg-laying, their four dung-usage groups (telecoprid, endocoprid, paracoprid, kleptocoprid), their ecological importance, and their introduction into Australia. Provide a term for each phrase taken from the article:
2.1.1 "plants ... first to colonise the area"
2.1.2 "change from one community to a different plant community"
2.1.3 "final species present in the area"
subQuestions.memoText:
2.1.1 Pioneer (species)
2.1.2 (Secondary) succession — NOT primary
2.1.3 Climax (community)
(1 mark each)

subQuestions.questionText: Telecoprid dung beetles can roll dung balls much heavier than themselves. The text states a telecoprid has a mass of 12 g and can push a ball up to 50 times its own weight. Use this information to calculate the mass of a dung ball. Show your working.
subQuestions.memoText: 12 g × 50 = 600 g (2 marks; unit not required).

subQuestions.questionText:
Figure 2.2 shows four different methods of dung usage by beetles at a dung pile, and Figure 2.3 shows two species that differ in dung usage (left: Aphodius, an endocoprid; right: Kheper, a telecoprid; both life size).
2.3.1 How does the behaviour of dung beetles illustrate the concept of interspecific competition?
2.3.2 Explain how the use of dung by the different types of dung beetle is an example of resource partitioning.
2.3.3 Compare and explain how the body structures of each of the two dung beetles in Figure 2.3 are adapted to their different use of dung.
(Refer to Figures 2.2 and 2.3 in the source booklet.)
subQuestions.memoText:
2.3.1 (3 marks): different species/types of beetle use the same resource (dung) at the same place and time; they have different behaviours to secure as much dung as possible and come into direct conflict with each other (e.g. kleptocoprids steal balls from telecoprids).
2.3.2 (2 marks): the beetles use the same resource (dung) in different ways and in different places (rolling it away, burying it beneath, feeding within it), so more individuals of different species can obtain dung to eat and breed in, and fewer beetles compete in one spot.
2.3.3 (4 marks — must compare both): Aphodius (endocoprid) is small, so it feeds within / pushes only small amounts of dung; it has small legs with few ridges and no shovel-shaped head structure for tunnelling. Kheper (telecoprid) is large, so it rolls large dung balls; it has larger, strongly ridged legs to grip the ground and a shovel-shaped head structure to dig a burrow.

subQuestions.questionText:
Figure 2.5 maps the movement of seven dung beetles (1–7) in and around a cow dung pile. Using the diagram and the information in the sources, give the number of a beetle (1–7) that fits the description of a(n):
(i) telecoprid
(ii) endocoprid
(iii) kleptocoprid
(Refer to Figure 2.5 in the source booklet.)
subQuestions.memoText:
(i) telecoprid — 1, 2, 5 or 6 (rolls a ball away from the pile in a straight line)
(ii) endocoprid — 3 or 4 (stays in the pile)
(iii) kleptocoprid — 7 (moves to another beetle's ball / track and steals it)
(1 mark each)

subQuestions.questionText:
Although dung beetles can occur in large groups in a single area, they are not socially organised.
2.5.1 Name ONE social insect that you have studied.
2.5.2 Discuss the social organisation of the insect you named in Question 2.5.1.
subQuestions.memoText:
2.5.1 (1 mark) Any one: termites / bees / wasps / ants.
2.5.2 (4 marks): roles are divided between different individuals (caste differentiation) with a single reproductive caste (e.g. queen); workers collect or cultivate food, care for the young and build/maintain the nest; soldiers defend the colony; this division of labour lets the colony control its environment far more than a solitary insect could; strong communication (e.g. pheromones, dances) passes information between members.

subQuestions.questionText: List FOUR ways in which dung beetles are important for maintaining a healthy ecosystem.
subQuestions.memoText: Any 4 (1 mark each): remove/clear dung from grazing fields (especially in summer); reduce fly breeding in dung, lowering disease and parasite loads; recycle nutrients by burying dung in the soil for plant growth; aerate the soil with their tunnels; keep buried carbon dioxide out of the atmosphere (limits global warming); bury and disperse seeds contained in the dung.

subQuestions.questionText: Even though dung beetles are important for ecosystem functioning, they do not get as much attention when it comes to conservation. Suggest why this is so.
subQuestions.memoText: Any 2 (1 mark each): they are small and rarely seen; many people dislike insects / find them unpleasant; living in dung makes people regard them as unhygienic; conservation focus tends to fall on charismatic species (e.g. bees, large vertebrates); dung and insects are poorly studied and understood; dung beetles are not endangered, so they are not prioritised.

subQuestions.questionText: Many species of dung beetle were considered for export to Australia. Suggest TWO criteria scientists would have used for selecting suitable types of beetle.
subQuestions.memoText: Any 2 (1 mark each): a larger beetle that uses a lot of dung efficiently; not a kleptocoprid; breeds/reproduces quickly; not invasive; does not eat native vegetation; does not transmit parasites or disrupt native food chains; adapted to the Australian climate and able to breed in cattle/sheep dung; able to disperse well.

subQuestions.questionText:
Refer to Sources A–G in the Source Material Booklet (definitions of traditional hunting; laws and religion; hunting as a 'rite of passage'; hunting in American culture; fox hunting in the UK; quotes; the Danish whale hunt, Japanese dolphin hunt and South African sport fishing). Consider the statement:

"Traditional hunting practices are still a valid part of modern society."

Using the source material and your own knowledge, discuss your opinion in an essay of 2½–3 pages. You are expected to: read the sources carefully; take a definite stand; plan your essay before writing (the plan is marked); present a debated argument using relevant information from Sources A–G plus your own Life Sciences knowledge; arrange the information to develop your argument; write in a scientifically appropriate way; and discuss at least nine different facts from the sources.
subQuestions.memoText:
Marked with the IEB essay rubric (40): Planning (6) — decision given, key points for and against developed, close use of source detail. Use of knowledge from sources (8) — up to ~9 source facts integrated to support the argument. Use of own knowledge (4). Content relevance (2). Quality of argument supporting the decision (8) — clear position, clear succinct reasoning, logical flow. Fairness — counter-opinions from the sources integrated (4). Presentation (4) — introduction and conclusion, paragraphing, transitions. Scientific merit (4) — mature tone, correct terminology.

Examples of usable facts —
FOR (still valid): traditions represent the values of a society and give a sense of belonging (A); the UN Human Rights Council and the SA Constitution protect the right to enjoy one's culture and heritage (B); Eaton argues hunting is fundamental to a male's maturing process and teaches compassion, self-control and sound judgement (C); hunting is integral to American heritage (D); fox hunting dates from the 15th century, has its own art and literature, supports the rural economy and creates jobs (E); an ex-UK PM favours fox hunting (E/F); the Faroese whale hunt is over 1 200 years old, the meat is shared equally, the government calls the method humane and the take (~800 of ~778 000 whales) sustainable (G); regulated hunting can keep populations below carrying capacity and fund conservation.
AGAINST (not valid): 'values' should not include killing and cruel practices are not justified merely by being traditions — e.g. FGM has been reformed (A); many religions and most of the UK public oppose hunting, and it is partially banned in the UK / banned in Scotland (B/E); the Maasai replaced lion hunting with the Maasai Olympics and fishing competitions have moved to catch-and-release (C/G); manhood is no longer earned by hunting (C); fox numbers are already low, foxes are minor pests (1–3% of losses) and hunting does not significantly control them (E); whales are highly social pod animals, are stressed and killed with knives, meat can carry high mercury and can be replaced with other food (G); modern society is more gender-neutral and hunting can drive species to extinction.
